subject: chemistry-1
question: In a hypothetical furnace demonstration, calcium carbonate decomposes completely: CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g). Using 44 g/mol as the molar mass of CO2, what mass of CO2 is released when 2 mol of CaCO3 decomposes?

options.text: 22 g, obtained by dividing the 44 g/mol molar mass between the 2 mol of CaCO3
200 g, because the 100 g/mol molar mass of CaCO3 is applied to the 2 mol
44 g, because one mole of CO2 leaves the solid no matter how large the sample is
88 g, because 2 mol of CO2 forms and each mole has a mass of 44 g

explanation:
The balanced equation has a 1:1 mole ratio of CaCO3 to CO2, so 2 mol of carbonate releases 2 mol of CO2. Converting moles to mass with the molar mass of the gas gives 2 mol x 44 g/mol = 88 g. The two-step pattern of moles of reactant, then mole ratio, then molar mass of the requested substance is the standard route for every mass-based stoichiometry calculation, and the molar mass used must belong to the substance being asked about.

ELI-10: Work in two steps. First use the equation's ratio: one CaCO3 releases one CO2, so 2 mol in means 2 mol of gas out. Then convert moles of gas to grams using the molar mass of that gas: 2 x 44 = 88 g. The common trap is grabbing the molar mass of the starting solid instead of the substance the question asks for.
